title: Lower limb peripheral arterial disease (PAD)
subject: cardiology
setting: Outpatient clinic, emergency department, vascular ward
summary: Confirm PAD with ABI 0.90 or less (toe-brachial index if ABI above 1.40); give single antiplatelet or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin, high-intensity statin, BP and smoking control, supervised exercise for claudication, and refer CLTI urgently and acute limb ischaemia as an emergency with IV heparin.

sections.title: Recognise and classify
items: Claudication: reproducible pain, cramping or fatigue in the buttock, thigh or calf on walking, relieved within about 10 minutes of rest. Many patients with PAD have atypical or no leg symptoms but still have high cardiovascular risk.

At increased risk (ACC/AHA): age 65 or more; age 50 to 64 with atherosclerotic risk factors, CKD or family history; under 50 with diabetes plus one other risk factor; known atherosclerosis in another bed.
Examine femoral, popliteal and pedal pulses, listen for bruits, and inspect legs and feet for hair loss, elevation pallor, dependent rubor, wounds, ulcers and gangrene.

Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI): ischaemic rest pain (forefoot, worse on elevation, eased by hanging the leg down), a non-healing wound or gangrene for more than 2 weeks with proven arterial disease. Stage with WIfI (wound, ischaemia, foot infection).

Acute limb ischaemia (under 2 weeks): pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paraesthesia and paralysis. Any sensory loss beyond the toes or muscle weakness means the limb is immediately threatened.
Differentials: spinal stenosis (relief by sitting or bending forward), nerve root pain, hip or knee arthritis, venous claudication, popliteal entrapment in young patients.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Resting ABI with Doppler: 0.90 or less abnormal (PAD), 0.91 to 0.99 borderline, 1.00 to 1.40 normal, above 1.40 non-compressible (common in diabetes and CKD).
ABI above 1.40: measure toe pressure and toe-brachial index (TBI 0.70 or less is abnormal).
Exertional leg symptoms with a normal or borderline resting ABI: exercise treadmill ABI.
Suspected CLTI: add toe pressure or TBI, transcutaneous oxygen pressure or skin perfusion pressure to judge perfusion and wound-healing potential.
Duplex ultrasound is the first-line anatomical test. Reserve CT angiography, MR angiography or catheter angiography for when revascularisation is being planned.
Baseline bloods (lipid profile, HbA1c, creatinine and eGFR, FBC) and ECG; look for coronary, carotid and aortic disease as clinically indicated.

sections.title: Cardiovascular and limb risk reduction (all patients)
items: Symptomatic PAD: single antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel 75 mg daily or aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily (ACC/AHA accepts aspirin 75 to 325 mg).

Symptomatic PAD at high ischaemic risk without high bleeding risk, and after lower-limb revascularisation: rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily reduces MACE and major limb events (ACC/AHA class 1; ESC class IIa).
Do not give full-dose anticoagulation for PAD alone (only for AF, VTE or another indication). Long-term DAPT without recent revascularisation has uncertain benefit.
Asymptomatic PAD: single antiplatelet is reasonable per ACC/AHA; ESC suggests aspirin may be considered mainly when diabetes is present.

High-intensity statin for all. ESC target LDL-C below 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) with at least 50% reduction; add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor if not at goal (ACC/AHA: add when LDL-C stays 70 mg/dL or more on maximal statin).

Blood pressure: ACE inhibitor or ARB preferred. ESC target SBP 120 to 129 mmHg if tolerated (below 140/90 mmHg in frail or very old patients); ACC/AHA target below 130/80 mmHg. Beta-blockers are not contraindicated in PAD.
Stop all tobacco: advise at every visit and offer varenicline, bupropion or nicotine replacement with counselling. Type 2 diabetes: SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven CV benefit.
Annual influenza and COVID-19 vaccination. Foot inspection at every visit, foot-care education, comprehensive foot examination at least yearly, and therapeutic footwear for high-risk feet.

sections.title: Claudication
items: Supervised exercise therapy first: intermittent walking to moderate or maximal claudication pain with rest periods, 30 to 45 minutes per session, at least 3 times a week for at least 12 weeks. A structured home-based walking programme is an effective alternative.
Cilostazol 100 mg twice daily improves walking distance. Contraindicated in heart failure of any severity; review at 3 months and stop if there is no useful benefit.
Pentoxifylline and chelation therapy are not recommended for claudication.
Revascularisation (endovascular, surgical or hybrid) is for functionally limiting claudication despite medical therapy and structured exercise, never to prevent progression in asymptomatic PAD.
Continue structured exercise after revascularisation to maintain walking performance.

sections.title: Acute limb ischaemia (emergency)
items: Acutely cold, painful, pulseless limb: urgent assessment of motor and sensory function and arterial and venous Doppler signals by a vascular specialist. Do not delay a threatened limb for imaging.
Give IV unfractionated heparin on diagnosis unless contraindicated (for example 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/h, adjusted to aPTT or anti-Xa).

Rutherford I (viable, no sensory or motor loss): urgent imaging and revascularisation. IIa (sensory loss limited to toes, no weakness): urgent revascularisation. IIb (sensory loss beyond toes, mild to moderate weakness): emergency revascularisation.
Rutherford III (anaesthetic, paralysed limb, no arterial or venous Doppler signal): irreversible; do not revascularise; primary amputation or palliation.
After reperfusion, monitor for compartment syndrome (fasciotomy), hyperkalaemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria and AKI.

Find the cause: ECG and rhythm monitoring for AF, echocardiography; consider graft or stent thrombosis, popliteal aneurysm, dissection, HIT, antiphospholipid syndrome and cancer-associated thrombosis.

sections.title: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
items: Refer urgently to a vascular multispecialty team; revascularise as soon as feasible to relieve rest pain, heal wounds and save a functional limb.
Evaluate revascularisation options before any amputation; map the great saphenous vein by ultrasound if bypass is possible.
Treat foot infection promptly with antibiotics, debridement and drainage; offload pressure for diabetic foot ulcers; provide structured wound care after revascularisation.
Primary amputation when life over limb is the priority (sepsis, metabolic derangement) or the limb is non-salvageable; choose the most distal level likely to heal.
Give adequate analgesia for rest pain; protect heels and avoid tight dressings.

sections.title: Follow-up
items: Every visit: symptoms, walking ability, pulses, full foot inspection, and progress on lipid, BP, glucose and smoking targets.
After endovascular treatment or vein bypass: ABI and arterial duplex at 1 to 3 months, then at 6 and 12 months, then yearly. New leg symptoms need ABI and duplex promptly.

After endovascular revascularisation, DAPT (low-dose aspirin plus clopidogrel) for 1 to 6 months is reasonable per ACC/AHA, weighing bleeding risk, before single antiplatelet or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Trusting a normal or high ABI in diabetes or CKD: calcified arteries give ABI above 1.40, so check toe pressures.
Starting cilostazol in a patient with heart failure.
Dismissing rest pain, ulcers or gangrene as poor circulation: CLTI carries high amputation and death rates and needs urgent referral.
Applying compression bandages for a presumed venous ulcer without checking the ABI.
Stopping the statin or antithrombotic therapy after a successful revascularisation.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.notes: ACC/AHA range 75 to 325 mg. Alternative: clopidogrel.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.notes: Single antiplatelet option in symptomatic PAD; short-term with aspirin after endovascular revascularisation.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban (vascular dose)
drugs.dose: 2.5 mg orally twice daily with aspirin 75 to 100 mg once daily
drugs.notes: Symptomatic PAD at high ischaemic risk, or after revascularisation once haemostasis is secure. Avoid with high bleeding risk or CrCl below 15 mL/min.

drugs.name: Atorvastatin
drugs.dose: 40 to 80 mg orally once daily (or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg once daily)
drugs.notes: High intensity for all patients; add ezetimibe 10 mg daily if LDL-C not at goal.

drugs.name: Cilostazol
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily, 30 minutes before or 2 hours after food
drugs.notes: Claudication only. Contraindicated in heart failure. 50 mg twice daily with strong CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 inhibitors. Stop if no benefit at 3 months.

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin
drugs.dose: 80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/h infusion titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa
drugs.notes: Acute limb ischaemia on diagnosis unless contraindicated.
